text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

text:
IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Among the brokers or registered employees at its Wall Street address, there are currently seven individuals with at least 3 or more public disclosures in the Central Registration Depository (CRD) known as BrokerCheck, a national database that tracks the background and disciplinary history of stockbrokers and other financial professional concerning customer complaints, regulatory or criminal events, and other financial disclosures (such as personal bankruptcy or tax liens).  This is significant, because, according to FINRA, most brokers have a clean history, with approximately 4% having been subject to at least one customer complaint, but only less than 0.41% with 3 or more BrokerCheck complaints. “The Institutional Sales & Trading Team has over 100 years of combined experience in both bull and bear markets, executing orders from broker/dealers, hedge funds and high net worth individuals. The firm makes markets in Exchange Listed, NASDAQ and OTC equities, both foreign and domestic, to ensure the highest possible quality executions. We have access to most exchanges, algorithmic strategies and dark pools, giving our customers unparalleled liquidity.” (emphasis added)

➡️Lets look at Paulson's regulatory history

✅Market Manipulation - SEC action dated Nov. 22, 2024

The SEC censured the firm, fined it $75,000, and ordered it to cease and desist from violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17a-8 thereunder. The SEC also ordered the firm to hire an independent anti-money laundering compliance consultant.

"In another example, in July 2021, Paulson filed a SAR in which the narrative stated that for May and June 2021, another broker-dealer’s trading volume with Paulson averaged nearly 25% of the shares outstanding in a security. The SAR narrative, however, failed to include all of the information required by FinCEN, including the name of the security at issue; the details of the broker-dealer’s trades in this security, such as the dates, amounts, and prices of the trades; the total trading volume in the security at issue as compared to the broker-dealer’s trading volume; Paulson’s relationship with the broker-dealer; whether Paulson had previously filed any related SARs; and any actions taken by Paulson." “As a further example, in June 2022, Paulson filed a SAR in which the narrative referenced a wash sale exception report that appeared to show day trading for the purpose of market manipulation. The SAR narrative, however, failed to include all of the information required by FinCEN, including the subject’s name; the details of the apparent wash sale trading, such as other broker-dealers involved, the subject security or securities, the dates, amounts and prices of the trading at issue, and why the trades appeared to be wash sales; whether Paulson had previously filed any related SARs; and any actions taken by Paulson.” [2]

✅FINRA Fine [3]:

"On May 20, 2024, FINRA filed a Letter of Acceptance, Waiver & Consent (AWC) alleging that Paulson Investment Company failed to file or timely file documents and information relating to seven public takedown offerings of securities.

The AWC alleged that Paulson Investment Company acted as placement agent for a biotechnology company in connection with a $100 million shelf offering of securities in March 2018, then participated in seven public takedown offerings for securities from this shelf offering in May 2018 and April 2019.

The firm allegedly also failed to establish and maintain a system of supervision reasonably designed to achieve compliance with FINRA Rule 5110’s filing and disclosure requirements.

Known as the Corporate Financing Rule, FINRA Rule 5110 requires members participating in a public offering to file documents concerning the underwriting terms and arrangements before the offering commences.

Why RMG can restart after the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment — and why it still hasn’t (yet). A legal breakdown:

The 10 Feb 2026 amendment to the IT Rules did not repeal or dilute the PROGA 2025 Act.
What it did was introduce a conditional statutory exception — not an automatic revival.

1️⃣ The baseline position: PROGA 2025's criminal prohibition

Under Section 5, PROGA 2025:
“No person shall offer, aid, abet, induce or otherwise engage in the offering of any online money game or online money gaming service.”

Violation attracts Section 9 penalties:

➡️ up to 3 years’ imprisonment and/or ₹1 crore fine.
This prohibition became effective from the date of Presidential assent (22 Aug 2025) — no rule-making required.

2️⃣ Why payments stopped — and why they matter:

Under Section 7, PROGA 2025:
“No bank, financial institution or payment intermediary shall engage in, permit, aid or facilitate any transaction towards payment for any online money gaming service.”
This made UPI, cards, wallets and gateways criminally exposed if they processed RMG transactions.
Hence the immediate, industry-wide payment freeze.

3️⃣ What the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment actually changed:

The amendment introduced the concept of a “permissible online real-money game” under the IT Rules framework.
Crucially, it says:

- A real-money game is not prohibited only if it is
• verified as permissible
• certified by a government-recognised Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO)
• compliant with prescribed safeguards.
This is an exception clause — not a repeal.

4️⃣ How this legally unlocks PROGA (if conditions are met)
Once a game is certified as “permissible” under the IT Rules:

It falls outside the definition of a prohibited “online money game”
(A) Section 5 PROGA no longer applies to that game,
(B) Section 7 payment ban no longer triggers
(C) Advertising restrictions tied to “online money games” also lift for that specific certified game
(D) No certification = PROGA ban continues in full force.

5️⃣ Why RMG hasn’t restarted at scale despite the amendment:

Because, as of now:
- SRO recognition is limited / evolving
- Certification is game-specific, not platform-wide
- Any misclassification risks criminal prosecution, not just regulatory fines
- Platforms will not operate on “interpretation” when jail liability exists.

6️⃣ Most important legal shift (often missed):

Earlier:
Courts decided skill vs chance post-facto.
Now:
Statutory gatekeeping precedes operation.
No SRO approval → no legality → no payments.

7️⃣ Bottom line:

The Feb 10, 2026 amendment did not “revive” RMG.
It created a narrow, conditional doorway.

RMG can restart only game-by-game, only after SRO certification, and only within IT Rules safeguards.

Until then, PROGA’s criminal prohibitions remain fully operative.
Law changed — but risk calculus didn’t.

April 4, 2026 | New Delhi: The Editors Guild of India is deeply concerned by both the contents and the underlying intent behind the Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026 (“Draft Amendments”), which were made public by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on March 30, 2026, with just a fortnight given for comments.
Prima facie, the amended rules and guidelines, whose stated purpose is to “strengthen compliance” and increase the effectiveness of regulatory oversight of content regulation mechanisms under Part III (Code of Ethics relating to Digital Media) of the IT Rules, 2021” appear to arm MeitY with sweeping powers of content regulation, sharply increases the compliance burden on digital intermediaries, and gives the executive overarching powers to block or take down content generated by  “non news publishers” and intermediaries. This will directly infringe the fundamental right to free speech guaranteed to all citizens under the Constitution and will have a chilling effect on freedom of expression and the airing of contrarian views, which are fundamental to an open and functional democracy.
Sub-rule (4) to Rule 3, which deals with due diligence obligations of intermediaries, now makes it mandatory on the part of intermediaries to comply with “any clarification, advisory, order, direction, standard operating procedure, code of practice or guideline issued by the ministry, by order in writing”. Failure to comply has been linked to loss of the safe harbour protection extended to intermediaries and platforms for user-generated content, under section 79 of the Information Technology Act. The absence of due process for the issuance of compliance orders and the complete lack of transparency in the process are deeply concerning.
Changes to Rule 14(2) and Rule 14(5) in the draft amendment also greatly widen the powers of the Inter-Departmental Committee (IDC). IDC, a central oversight body constituted under Rule 14 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, was specifically created to hear grievances and complaints against digital content. Now, the IDC has been empowered to deal with and “matter” – a generalisation which arms the body to consider virtually any issue, in the absence of any definition of what constitutes a “matter”. Other provisions devolve rulemaking powers entirely to the executive branch, removing the window for legislative oversight provided under the IT Act.
The EGi calls on the government to urgently review or recall the draft rules, and engage in more constructive consultations with all sections of stakeholders and take on board valid concerns and objections.
Warm regards,
Sanjay Kapoor, President
Raghavan Srinivasan, General Secretary
Teresa Rehman, Treasurer

🔥 𝗜𝗡 𝟭𝟵𝟳𝟴, 𝗟𝗟𝗥 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗗 𝗕𝗘𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝟳 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗠𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗥𝗧 𝗝𝗨𝗗𝗚𝗘𝗦.
𝟰𝟴 𝗬𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗦 𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗥, 𝗬𝗔𝗝𝗔𝗧 𝗞𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗥 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗗 𝗕𝗘𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝟵 — 𝗢𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗔𝗠𝗘 𝗗𝗘𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡:
𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗔𝗡 “𝗜𝗡𝗗𝗨𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗬”?

In 1978, Late Sh. H.L. Kumar, Founder Editor-in-Chief of Labour Law Reporter, appeared before the 7-Judge Bench in 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 & 𝗦𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗕𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝘃. 𝗔. 𝗥𝗮𝗷𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗮.

That landmark decision gave Indian labour jurisprudence the 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 and 𝗗𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗡𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 for Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

➠ 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲.

𝗦𝗵. 𝗬𝗮𝗷𝗮𝘁 𝗞𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗿 — Advocate, Supreme Court of India & Editor, Labour Law Reporter — represented one of the parties before the 9-Judge Bench in 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗨.𝗣. 𝘃. 𝗝𝗮𝗶 𝗕𝗶𝗿 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗵, CA No. 897/2002.

✦ 𝗬𝗔𝗝𝗔𝗧 𝗞𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗥’𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

Relying on 𝗻𝗼𝘀𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗿 𝗮 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗶𝘀, it was argued that “industry” cannot be tested merely by the manner in which an organised activity is carried on.

➝ The 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆 must also bear analogy to trade or business.
➝ The activity must be considered in the context of material goods, wealth or material services.
➝ The interpretation of “material services” in 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗷𝘂𝗻𝗴 𝗛𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 was supported.

❶ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗝𝗜’𝗦 𝗢𝗣𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗢𝗡

Chief Justice Surya Kant, for himself and Justices Satish Chandra Sharma, Alok Aradhe and Vipul M. Pancholi, gave renewed emphasis to the “nature of activity”.

It should possess a 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗿 analogous to trade or business, with emphasis equal to the employer-employee basis. Significantly, the opinion described this reformulation as 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹.

❷ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥 𝗢𝗣𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦

↳ Justice B.V. Nagarathna: 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 remains good law and binding.
↳ Justice P.S. Narasimha: declined to adjudicate its validity in view of repeal of the ID Act and introduction of the IR Code.
↳ Justice Dipankar Datta, with Justice Ujjal Bhuyan: Reference not maintainable; 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 remains good law.
↳ Justice Joymalya Bagchi: Reference maintainable, but the 1978 ratio should be retained; Section 2(p) of the IR Code should be interpreted independently.

➤ 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗧𝗔𝗞𝗘𝗔𝗪𝗔𝗬

For pending disputes under the ID Act, 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 continues to govern. The definition of “industry” under Section 2(p) of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 must be interpreted on its own terms.

For LLR, this is more than a judgment — it is a 𝟰𝟴-𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗰𝘆: from Late Sh. H.L. Kumar before 7 Judges to Sh. Yajat Kumar before 9 Judges.

@IITKgp hosted the Digital India Talk Show at the Kalidas Auditorium, in association with the National e-Governance Division @NeGD_GoI, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India, bringing together experts, faculty members, and participants for insightful conversations on India’s evolving digital ecosystem and citizen-centric governance.

The programme was convened by Dr. Kaushal Kumar Bhagat, who delivered the welcome address and set the context for the deliberations. Prof. Kamal Lochan Panigrahi, Dean (Administration), IIT Kharagpur, highlighted the importance of such initiatives in strengthening awareness and engagement around India’s digital transformation, while Mr. Ajeet Kumar, Deputy General Manager, NeGD, shared perspectives on key initiatives under Digital India.

The technical sessions offered valuable insights into key pillars of India’s digital public infrastructure, including DigiLocker and Entity Locker, UMANG and myScheme, API Setu, MeriPehchaan, and UX4G, along with important discussions on cybersecurity and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The sessions explored how secure digital credentials, integrated public services, interoperability, unified authentication, data protection and citizen-centric design are transforming the delivery of public services.

The initiative provided participants with a deeper understanding of the technologies and frameworks that enable more accessible, secure, and efficient digital governance across the country.

Through such engagements, IIT Kharagpur continues to contribute to capacity building, awareness, and meaningful dialogue around digital governance and emerging technologies, supporting the larger vision of an inclusive and digitally empowered India.

Content creator and activist @shristhikhanna has claimed that her Instagram account was legally blocked in India following a government notice.

In a social media post, Khanna wrote, "My Instagram account was legally banned by the Government of India. It is crazy the resources being allocated to kill free speech in every sense, including on social media."

In a video explaining the development, she alleged that she was not provided with prior notice or detailed reasons for the action. Khanna said the account, which had more than 100,000 followers, became inaccessible in India after the alleged government order.

She also criticised what she described as selective enforcement, questioning why accounts issuing rape threats, death threats, and sharing deepfake content remain online despite being reported. Khanna further claimed that discussions on issues such as Palestine, disability justice, environmental justice, queer rights, and criticism of the government face restrictions on social media in India.

She urged her followers to connect with her through her other social media platforms, saying they could find links in her profile, and ended her message by reiterating her support for Palestine.

Free speech is easy when you agree with it.

That’s not the test.

Elon told Bill Maher, "Free speech only matters when it’s someone you don’t like saying something you don’t like."

🚨 Is the Indian Government Turning X into Its Personal Censor?

Read how in 2026:
India just slashed the takedown deadline for “unlawful” content on X, Meta, YouTube & others from 36 hours to just 3 hours (effective Feb 20). One missed deadline? Heavy penalties.
That’s not regulation — that’s leverage.

With 1 billion+ internet users, India has weaponised its market size + Section 69A/IT Rules + the new “Sahyog” portal (where thousands of officials can directly order blocks). 

Real examples:
•  July 2025: Govt ordered X to block 2,355 accounts in one go — including Reuters and Reuters World. X publicly called it “press censorship” and said the order came with a 1-hour ultimatum and zero justification.
•  Feb 2026: X account of journalist Azad Essa (Middle East Eye) was geo-blocked in India after critical reporting on India-Israel ties.
•  Ongoing: X has blocked thousands of posts and hundreds of accounts under Indian orders, even while suing the government in court (and losing some rounds on free-speech grounds because X is a “foreign entity”).

X’s own Global Affairs team has repeatedly flagged “deep concern” over these mass blocking orders. Elon Musk’s platform — built on free speech — is being forced to play by rules no other major democracy enforces so aggressively.

The irony? The same government that once clashed with old Twitter now demands faster, wider compliance… while critics (journalists, opposition voices, even satire) disappear behind geo-blocks or full bans.

India isn’t just using X.
It’s exploiting the platform’s global reach to control the narrative inside its borders — and beyond.

Free speech isn’t free when one country can hit the mute button faster than you can say “Sahyog.” 
BJP attempting to make a “Om Birla” out of X, trying to mute the opposition whenever they open their mouth to criticise. 

If this is not digital authoritarianism, what is?

Amid heightened tensions and a heavy police presence in Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan state in India, the local administration has begun demolishing a 44-year-old historic mosque. The operation was carried out on Sunday (June 7) to remove the historic Noorani Mosque, located in the Malviya Nagar area of Jaipur.

The four-story Noorani Mosque located in Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, India, is being demolished by the authorities as part of a road-widening project. In connection with the operation, internet services across the city were suspended for 24 hours, and extensive security measures were put in place.

The Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) claims that the mosque was constructed illegally on leased land. However, the mosque committee has rejected this allegation, stating that the land was legally purchased from a housing society in 1981 before the structure was built.

A large number of police personnel have been deployed in and around the area, drone surveillance is being conducted, and restrictive orders remain in effect throughout the operation. The mosque committee and several opposition lawmakers have criticized the move, alleging that proper procedures were not followed.

Authorities stated that the temporary internet shutdown was imposed to prevent the spread of rumors and misinformation and to maintain law and order during the demolition process. So far, the operation has remained peaceful, with no reports of violence or unrest.

1500th Anniversary of the the Birth of Holy Prophet Muhammad SAWS 

*Highlights of Islam in each Islamic (Hijri) century after the time of Prophet Muhammad (SAWS).

1: 1st Century AH (1st to 100 AH):
-Compilation of the Quran: The final written text of the Holy Quran was standardized and copied during Caliph Uthman's rule.
-Rapid Expansion: Muslim rule spread quickly across the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of Central Asia.
-Early Leadership: The era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the start of the Umayyad Dynasty shaped early governance.

2: 2nd Century AH (101 to 200 AH):
-Rise of Baghdad: The Abbasid Caliphate took power and moved the capital to Baghdad, starting a cultural boom.
-School of Law: Major Islamic legal traditions (Madhhabs), like the Hanafi and Maliki schools, were founded and organized.
-Translation Movement: Scholars began translating ancient scientific and philosophical texts into Arabic.

3: 3rd Century AH (201 to 300 AH):
-Hadith Collection: Major verified books of sayings of the Prophet, like Sahih al-Bukhari, were finalized.
-Scientific Growth: Muslim scientists like Al-Khwarizmi made huge breakthroughs in mathematics and algebra.
-Political Splitting: Regional Muslim rulers gained more local power as the central Abbasid grip weakened.

4: 4th Century AH (301 to 400 AH):
-Fatimid Rise: The Fatimid Caliphate was established in North Africa and later founded Cairo and Al-Azhar University.
-Golden Spain: Muslim Spain (Al-Andalus) became a major European center of art, learning, and philosophy.
-Theology Defined: Major Sunni creed schools (Ash'ari and Maturidi) were formalized to explain Islamic beliefs.

5: 5th Century AH (401 to 500 AH):
-Spread of Sufism: Islamic mysticism and spiritual orders became organized and widespread through teachers like Al-Ghazali.
-Seljuk Rule: The Seljuk Turks united large parts of the Sunni Muslim world under a new military power.
-The Crusades Begin: European Christian armies invaded the Levant, starting centuries of holy wars in the region.

6: 6th Century AH (501 to 600 AH):
-Saladin's Victory: Muslim leader Salahuddin Ayyubi united Muslims and recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 CE.
-Philosophical Heights: Thinkers like Ibn Rushd (Averroes) wrote deep commentaries on philosophy and religion.
-Missionary Spread: Traders and Sufis peacefully brought Islam further into parts of India and Sub-Saharan Africa.

7: 7th Century AH (601 to 700 AH):
 -Mongol Devastation: Mongol armies invaded and destroyed Baghdad in 1258 CE, ending the Abbasid Caliphate.
-Battle of Ain Jalut: Mamluk forces stopped the Mongol advance in Egypt and protected remaining Islamic lands.
-Mongol Conversions: Many Mongol rulers eventually accepted Islam, turning conquerors into patrons of the faith.

8: 8th Century AH (701 to 800 AH):
-Rise of the Ottomans: A small Turkish principality began growing in Anatolia, laying roots for the Ottoman Empire.
-New Sociology: Scholar Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah, creating the foundation for modern sociology and history.
-Global Travel: Explorer Ibn Battuta traveled through the entire Muslim world and wrote detailed journals.

9: 9th Century AH (801 to 900 AH): 
-Conquest of Constantinople: Sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 CE, making it the Ottoman capital (Istanbul).
-Timurid Art: The Timurid dynasty created breathtaking architecture, miniature paintings, and poetry in Central Asia.
-Safavid Order: The Safavid religious order grew in Persia, setting the stage for a major Shiite empire.

10: 10th Century AH (901 to 1000 AH): 
-Mughal Empire: Babur founded the Mughal Empire, bringing a rich era of Islamic culture to South Asia.
-Three Empires: The Islamic world was dominated by three powerful and wealthy states: the Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals.
-Maritime Spread: Islam spread deeply into Southeast Asia (like Indonesia and Malaysia) through peaceful trade.

11: 11th Century AH (1001 to 1100 AH): 
-Architectural Peak: The Mughal Empire built world-famous monuments, including the Taj Mahal in India.
-Law Codification: Emperor Aurangzeb commissioned the Fatawa-e-Alamgiri, a massive guide on Islamic law.
-Scholarly Depth: Local Islamic schools and independent local scholars thrived across all three empires.

12: 12th Century AH (1101 to 1200 AH):
-Political Decline: The major gunpowder empires started losing military and economic power to rising European states.
-Reform Movements: Scholars like Shah Waliullah in India tried to revive and purify Islamic teachings.
-Wahhabi Movement: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab started a strict reform movement in the Arabian Peninsula.

13: 13th Century AH (1201 to 1300 AH): 
-Colonial Rule: European powers took over large portions of the Muslim world, from India to North Africa.
-Armed Resistance: Muslims fought back against foreign invaders with major anti-colonial uprisings.
-Modern Thought: Reformers like Jamal al-Din al-Afghani discussed how Islamic societies could adapt to modernity.

14: 14th Century AH (1301 to 1400 AH):
-End of the Caliphate: The Ottoman Empire fell after World War I, and the official Caliphate was abolished in 1924.
-New Nations: Modern, independent Muslim-majority nation-states were born across the globe.
-Islamic Revival: Political and social movements arose to bring Islamic values back into public life.

15: 15th Century AH (1401 to Present):
-Global Diaspora: Millions of Muslims migrated to live and build communities in Western countries.
-Digital Islam: The internet and social media transformed how Islamic knowledge is shared and taught globally.
-Demographic Growth: Islam became the fastest-growing major religion, with populations expanding rapidly worldwide.

🚨 Terrifying Natural Disaster on the China-Nepal Border: What is the Truth?
​The horrifying video going viral on social media is not due to a broken dam, but rather a devastating flash flood and mudslide that occurred near Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border.
​📍 Where and How Did It Happen?
​Location: The incident took place in the border area between Nepal and China's Tibet Autonomous Region, near the Bhotekoshi/Lhende River.
​Cause: According to initial reports, a mild earthquake occurred in the region, followed by landslides and ice-rock avalanches crashing into the river. This blocked the water flow, causing a terrifying mudslide and flash flood that swept over the Chinese border and Nepali settlements in mere seconds.
​💥 Casualties and Damages:
​Human Losses and Missing Persons: Dozens of people have died, while hundreds of tourists, locals, and security personnel (including police and military whose barracks were washed away) are missing. The missing include foreign tourists alongside Nepali citizens.
​Damage in China: The buildings, vehicles, and trade routes of Gyirong Port on the Chinese side (shown in the video) were completely submerged in water and mud, disrupting the communication system entirely.
​Damage in Nepal: Several villages, bridges, roads (approximately 25 kilometers of road network), and multiple hydropower projects were reduced to rubble inside Nepalese territory.
​🌐 Impacted Countries:
​China and Nepal: Their crucial shared overland trade route and bilateral transit corridor are completely paralyzed.

*58 arrests in global effort to dismantle West African organized crime groups*

_INTERPOL-coordinated operation leads to the identification of 263 suspects_

*LYON, France –* An eight-month operation targeting West African organized crime groups has led to 58 arrests and the identification of 263 suspects.

Operation Jackal IV (November 2025 – June 2026) aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution.

The operation, which brought together 22 countries from six continents, is a response to the escalating global threat posed by West African criminal networks – such as the Black Axe and other similar groups. These groups are responsible for a significant share of the world's cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance scams, cryptocurrency and investment scams or business email compromise fraud, as well as other serious and violent crimes. 

During the operation, INTERPOL facilitated cross-border coordination and intelligence sharing, conducted analysis, supported operational activities and provided specialized training to enhance international money laundering investigations. 

 ➡️ 🔗 https://t.co/rWGz2MPJ4D

Tomonobu Kaya, Director of the INTERPOL Financial Crime and Anti-Corruption Centre, said:
_“Operation Jackal IV demonstrates the power of international cooperation. By following illicit financial flows across borders, we are attacking the very lifeblood of organized crime and making it increasingly difficult for criminal networks to profit from their activities.”_ 

*Emerging threats and operational successes: Crime-as-a-Service, sextortion and scams* 

Due to the complexity of financial crime, many cases from Operation Jackal IV remain under investigation, however, preliminary outcomes include: 

* *Argentina:* 196 individuals were identified for their role in a major Crime-as-a-Service network, suspected of providing website domains and money laundering support to West African organized crime groups. The investigation led to 17 arrests. An INTERPOL Operational Support Team (OST) was deployed to assist the operation, providing analytical support on seized data, identifying criminal networks and suspects, and engaging with international partners to advance ongoing investigative leads.

* *South Africa:* Authorities raided seven locations in Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries. The criminal network operated an elaborate structure, with members designated as "conversion" or "retention" agents and tasked with different stages of the scam. An INTERPOL OST was also deployed locally to support South African law enforcement authorities who seized USD 2.67 million, blocked 257 bank accounts and arrested 39 individuals.

* *Italy:* One individual was identified in relation to a pan-European money laundering network that used shell companies, remittance services and cash withdrawals to obscure fund origins. A single account laundered EUR 845,000 (USD 736,000) across 560 transactions using 20 different financial instruments.

* *Romania:* Authorities dismantled a criminal group running a sophisticated investment scam via a call centre that touted high returns in stocks or cryptocurrencies. Victims’ money was diverted to electronic wallets controlled by the perpetrators, resulting in an estimated EUR 143 million stolen and laundered globally. Police arrested 11 individuals and seized approximately EUR 330,000 (USD 379,000) in cash and cryptocurrency, six real estate properties and several luxury watches.

Beyond individual cases, Operation Jackal IV also enabled the analysis of critical and emerging trends, including a rise in West African organized crime groups using sextortion to target minors, with victims as young as 14. 🚨 UPDATE — NEPAL: DEATH TOLL SURGES AS SCALE OF HIMALAYAN DISASTER EMERGES
The tragedy unfolding along the Nepal–Tibet border is worsening dramatically.
Nepal Police now report at least 95 people confirmed dead after Wednesday morning's catastrophic flash flood tore through the Bhote Koshi and downstream river systems. At least 63 injured survivors have been rescued and hospitalized.
But the confirmed deaths tell only part of the story.
Hundreds remain missing.
The Nepal Tourism Board initially reported 384 tourists and travelers out of contact, including 291 foreign nationals. Government figures indicate hundreds of foreigners, security personnel and others remain unaccounted for, meaning the toll could rise substantially.
Among the missing are tourists and pilgrims from numerous countries, including India, the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia. Many were traveling toward Mount Kailash in Tibet or Gosainkunda in Nepal.
Nepal's security forces have also suffered heavily, with police, Armed Police Force and Nepal Army personnel reported missing after posts and barracks were overwhelmed.
The disaster appears to have begun high in the Himalayan border region.
A preliminary scientific assessment suggests an ice-and-rock avalanche blocked the Lhende River, allowing water to accumulate before suddenly breaking loose into the Bhote Koshi system. Authorities are investigating whether a glacial lake also played a role. An earthquake was recorded in the wider region, but the precise chain of events remains under investigation.
Witnesses described a wall of water, mud and debris descending through narrow Himalayan valleys with virtually no warning.
Timure, near the Rasuwagadhi border crossing with China, was devastated. Buildings, markets, police posts and infrastructure were swept away. More than 300 vehicles and trucks waiting near the customs checkpoint were reportedly carried away.
The flood continued downstream, destroying or damaging settlements, bridges, highways, communications infrastructure and hydropower facilities.
Nepal's warning system was also overwhelmed. Officials say automatic monitoring stations in the upper Bhote Koshi were swept away before they could transmit alerts.
Helicopters, soldiers, police, medical teams and emergency personnel are now operating across an enormous Himalayan disaster zone, but destroyed roads, severed communications, unstable terrain and continuing flood danger are complicating rescue efforts.
And this is no longer solely a Nepalese catastrophe.
Across the border in Tibet, Chinese authorities report at least three people dead and 265 missing in Gyirong.
That puts the currently confirmed death toll on both sides of the border at at least 98, while hundreds remain missing.
Nepal has requested international assistance as rescuers race against time.
The figures remain provisional. Earlier Wednesday, Nepal was reporting fewer than 20 deaths. Hours later, police were reporting 95.
For hundreds of families in Nepal, Tibet and around the world, there is now an agonizing wait for news.
95 confirmed dead in Nepal.
At least 3 dead in Tibet.
Hundreds missing.
Entire communities devastated.
And rescuers are still trying to reach areas from which almost no information has emerged.

Order: Another matter of concern which has been brought to the notice of the court relates to the effective and smooth functioning of the committee. This court has been apprised that consequent upon the constitution of the Integrated Coordination Group, there is a substantial overlap in the composition of the committee and the Integrated Coordination Group, with several of the same senior functionaries being members of both bodies. We make it clear and emphasize that the Integrated Coordination Group has been formed by way of an internal arrangement for smooth and seamless conduct of the requisite exercise within the government departments and in no manner impinges upon the domain of the committee. What a crock. Daisy-chain logic. NCAA is enjoined → SEC has historically coordinated with NCAA on eligibility policy and supported NCAA positions in litigation → SEC adopts its own eligibility rule → therefore SEC was acting “in concert” with NCAA → therefore the SEC’s rule is attributable to NCAA → therefore NCAA is in contempt . . . That is an awful lot of “therefores” carrying an awful lot of doctrinal weight. If only that's how contempt works. It doesn't. The underlying injunction is subject to strict construction, and you still have to prove that the NCAA intentionally, knowingly, and purposefully violated the actual command of the order. SEC's involvement is a non sequitur. Institutional alignment, common policy objectives, and historical coordination do not get you there.

text:
🚨 TAX ALERT: Time-barred recovery suit cannot be revived by a payment made after limitation expired
🔹 What Happened: The Assessee claimed recovery of Rs.14,12,063/- towards paper supplied under invoices, relying on a subsequent cheque payment. The Court found that the last invoice was dated 08.11.2014 and the three-year limitation period had already expired before the alleged part-payment.

🔍 Key Takeaways:
Limitation: A money-recovery suit based on invoices carries a three-year limitation period; a payment made after expiry does not revive limitation.

Section 19: A fresh period starts only where partpayment/acknowledgment is made before expiry of the prescribed period.

Cheque  revival: A cheque issued after the debt had become time-barred could not constitute discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. Consequently, the recovery claim and interest were rejected.
⚖️ Legal Reference: Sections 3 & 19, Limitation Act, 1963 | Section 139, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 | CS (COMM.) No.300/2025, decided on 29.07.2026

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

The Union government’s draft Seeds Bill 2025, now open for public comments until 11 December, arrives not a day too soon. From counterfeit packets in village markets to procurement disputes at mandis, the chain between breeder and farmer has too many weak links.

For Punjab, where seed quality, FCI norms, and groundwater stress intersect, if not collide, every season, this Bill is more than a compliance document. It is a chance to rebuild trust in the most basic input of agriculture.

How is it better than the old law?

Three design shifts from the Seeds Act of 1966 deserve unambiguous support.

First, universal registration of varieties. The 1966 Act essentially regulated only ‘notified’ kinds, leaving a grey market of truthfully labelled seeds outside meaningful oversight. The draft moves toward mandatory registration for all new varieties and a pathway for deemed registration of existing ones. If implemented with predictable timelines and transparent criteria, this closes the back door through which poor-quality seed has circulated for decades.

Second, traceability and digital oversight. The draft emphasises traceability— already feasible through platforms that assign a scannable identity to each lot from breeder to dealer. That lets a farmer verify authenticity at the counter and allows regulators to trace a bad lot swiftly up the chain. Traceability should not be a slogan; it must become a farmer’s everyday tool. Make it mandatory at scale, standardise the QR/barcode, and integrate it with e-invoices so that one scan reveals who produced, processed, stored, and sold the seed, and when.

Third, smarter penalties with measured decriminalisation. Minor technical lapses should not land honest actors in criminal court; serious fraud should. The draft’s graded penalties, with steep fines and custodial terms for spurious and unregistered seed, are a clear improvement over the token fines of the 1966 law. The promise is a system that is both business-friendly and farmer‑protective—if enforcement stays sharp.

Two related moves are consequential for Punjab. One is the shift from a state-by-state dealer licensing culture to centralised accreditation/recognition. That may cut duplication for multi-state firms, but it also risks hollowing out the “last mile” unless states retain day-to-day inspection teeth. The other is price oversight “in emergent situations”. That clause matters in the sowing window, when speculation can shut smallholders out of quality seed.

Federal design at the last mile

The August ruling of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which held that states cannot ban centrally notified hybrid paddy, was a reminder that seed regulation sits across the Centre-state seam. Punjab has since hardened deterrence at its end, making the sale of spurious seeds a non-bailable, cognisable offence, reflecting accumulated anger in the countryside at fly-by-night operators. Industry protests aside, the message from Chandigarh is clear: the deterrent must be felt in the marketplace.

The draft national law should recognise this reality instead of flattening it. Keep national registration and central accreditation if you must—but codify concurrent enforcement powers for states: surprise sampling, seizure, prosecution, and the ability to prescribe local storage and display conditions. Delhi can set standards; inspectors in Moga and Muktsar will enforce them.

Farmers’ vantage point: performance and procurement

From a farmer’s field, regulation is judged by three blunt questions: Did the seed perform? If not, who pays? And will the crop be procured on fair terms?

The draft is strong at the pre-market gate (registration and traceability) and on deterrence. It is notably weaker on compensation when registered seed underperforms despite adoption of the recommended package of practices. Punjab’s last two seasons underlined why this gap matters: disruptive weather, discolouration and moisture contests at mandis, and a milling reluctance toward some hybrids have turned quality disputes into income shocks.

The fix is straightforward. Create a time-bound, no-fault compensation window for clear seed failures, financed by a blend of mandatory manufacturer insurance, a small cess on registrations, and state top-ups in disaster years. Publish the yield-loss formula up front; do not force a small farmer to litigate against a corporate legal team. At the same time, institutionalise pre-season coordination among the Agriculture Ministry, FCI/DFPD, and states on uniform procurement specifications, with a hybrid-specific annexure and pre-declared relaxations for flood years. Let seed standards and procurement norms talk to each other before the first bag is sold.

Let FPOs co-brand seed

Earlier seed‑bill drafts recognised a farmer’s right to save, use, exchange and sell farm‑saved seed, with one caveat: it cannot be sold under a brand name.

The intent was to block quasi‑commercial masquerading without quality assurance. But the rise of Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) changes the calculus. The Union government wants FPOs to aggregate, process, and market produce; it funds them and extends credit and tax support for precisely that reason. If the final Seeds Act mechanically extends a “no brand” caveat to FPO‑aggregated seed, it would hobble a flagship reform.

The harmonising path is clear: permit FPO co-branding of farm-saved seed provided three conditions are met. First, lots must pass notified minimum standards in an accredited lab. Second, full traceability, including grower IDs and storage logs that must be uploaded to the national portal. Third, liability must sit with the FPO’s board for false claims, not with individual members. That keeps out fly-by-night branding while letting farmer institutions move up the value chain.

Dealer liability, without scapegoating the honest

Punjab has thousands of small input dealers who act as the farmer’s first line of advice and supply. They cannot become the system’s whipping boy for failures they did not cause.

The law should adopt a manufacturer-first liability rule on germination and genetic purity for factory-sealed packs, while giving dealers a safe harbour if they sell sealed lots, meet prescribed storage conditions, keep traceable invoices, and hand over required samples during inspections. Penal exposure should bite dealers who tamper, knowingly misbrand, or operate outside the accredited chain. That keeps deterrence where it belongs—on those who cheat—without driving legitimate retailers out of business.

Traceability as a price stabiliser, not just a cop’s tool

If the Centre retains emergency price-control powers, anchor them in transparent triggers captured by the traceability system: inventory-to-sowing-window ratios, abnormal interstate price spreads, and unusual movement patterns. Public dashboards would discipline prices before official fiat is needed, and they would help states intervene in time. Let the QR on a packet be both a shield against fraud and a signal for markets.

Water‑wise seed choices backed by procurement

For Punjab, seed policy is also water policy. Short-duration, water-efficient paddy, as well as non-paddy kharif options, must get fast-track registration and agronomy support.

But farmers will not switch varieties or crops unless procurement policy aligns. That means assured purchase pathways for water-saving options, predictable miller acceptance for hybrids, and extension support that links seed choice to groundwater outcomes. Otherwise, the rational farmer will cling to long-duration staples that mills prefer and FCI buys on familiar specs.

It is essential to stitch seed regulation to FCI procurement policy for hybrid paddy so that what farmers sow confidently in June is not rejected quibblingly in October.

Minor tweaks before enactment: a Punjab‑first checklist

Keep central registration, but write state enforcement powers into the statute.

Clarify the liability chain: manufacturer first; dealer safe harbour for sealed, properly stored, traceable stock; strict penalties for tampering and misbranding.

Make compensation real with a time‑bound, no‑fault window and a published formula.

Hard‑wire coordination with FCI on uniform specs and a hybrid‑specific annexure, with pre‑declared relaxations in disaster years.

Use traceability to improve competition and price discovery, not merely to police.

Greenlight FPO co‑branding under standards‑plus‑traceability, with board‑level liability.

Invest in accredited seed labs and risk‑based inspections so enforcement is fast, fair and science‑led.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Prime Minister @andyburnham and Foreign Secretary @Ed_Miliband : how much longer will Britain remain silent?

For three years the father of my two sons, and Pakistan’s former Prime Minister, Imran Khan, has been brutally penalised by his political opponents, in a personal vendetta by Army Chief, Asim Munir,  which according to the UN,  amounts to torture and which  is now taking a potentially fatal toll on his physical and mental health. 

He has endured 3 years of solitary confinement. For nearly ten months now his family has been denied contact with him. He has been deprived of the most basic human contact, denied access to books, lawyers and doctors.

The international human-rights standards are unequivocal. Under the UN’s Nelson Mandela Rules, solitary confinement lasting more than 15 consecutive days is prohibited and amounts to torture.

He has endured this treatment not for 15 days, but for three years.

Pakistan’s own Supreme Court has now intervened: ordering comprehensive  medical treatment, access to his personal doctor, regular family visits and twice-weekly calls with his sons.

Yet those orders are being defied.

This is no longer simply a Pakistani political matter. It is a human-rights emergency.

He has deep and lifelong ties to Britain. He studied at Oxford University, captained Oxford University cricket and spent years playing county cricket in England. His relationship with this country stretches back more than half a century. His charitable activities were internationally recognised, and  include building the only free cancer hospital in Pakistan as well as a university.

His sons, my two boys, Sulaiman and Kasim, are British citizens. They have been forced to watch their father’s health decline from thousands of miles away, prevented from visiting him, denied visas, publicly threatened by government officials with arrest themselves, and even denied court-mandated regular phone calls. 

I have repeatedly appealed to the UK government to intervene. Purported attempts at back channelling have evidently failed. The previous Foreign Secretary @DavidLammy informed me in writing that Britain would not  intervene if my sons, British citizens, are arrested when they travel to Pakistan to visit their father. 

 @FCDOGovUK: Britain must now speak out publicly and unequivocally. Demand that Pakistan comply with its own Supreme Court;  restore Imran Khan’s medical access, his right to see his family, end his prolonged isolation and uphold his fundamental human rights.

Pakistan is a Commonwealth country. Britain has a long and proud tradition of standing against arbitrary detention, inhumane treatment and the denial of fundamental rights. Those principles mean very little if we invoke them only selectively and neglect them when inconvenient.
This an appeal to the new Burnham government  to please now do the right thing.

Jemima is right. But after three years, another expression of “concern” will achieve nothing.

The people responsible must finally face consequences that reach where power actually matters: money, assets, travel, trade privileges and international support.

@10DowningStreet @andyburnham @Ed_Miliband @FCDOGovUK:

Britain should lead a coordinated UK–EU–US response and make clear that there will be a material price for torture, prolonged isolation, denial of medical care and defiance of Pakistan’s own courts.

Public condemnation alone is not enough.

Authoritarian power structures can survive international embarrassment. What they cannot so easily ignore are:

• targeted asset freezes
• visa and travel bans
• scrutiny of overseas assets and financial interests
• suspension of assistance or training benefiting abusive state institutions
• human-rights conditions attached to diplomatic and security cooperation
• review of preferential trade arrangements where their human-rights conditions are being violated

The UK already has a Global Human Rights sanctions regime specifically capable of targeting individuals involved in torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.

The EU has the same power: asset freezes and travel bans for those responsible for serious human-rights abuses.

So use them.

Pakistan is also the EU’s largest GSP+ beneficiary. Those extraordinary trade preferences are not a charitable gift. They are explicitly tied to compliance with international conventions on human rights, good governance and the rule of law.

If those conditions can be systematically breached with no consequence, then what exactly are the conditions worth?

This is the fundamental mistake the democratic world keeps making with Pakistan:

issuing statements while preserving every privilege.

Trade continues.
Cooperation continues.
Access continues.
International legitimacy continues.

And therefore the cost of repression remains close to zero.

Do not punish ordinary Pakistanis. Protect humanitarian, health and education assistance.

But those ordering, facilitating or covering up serious abuses should understand that the democratic world is no longer a safe harbour for their wealth, travel, influence or impunity.

Investigate responsibly. Establish individual responsibility. Then sanction those for whom the evidence meets the legal threshold.

Because if credible allegations of torture can persist, Supreme Court safeguards can allegedly be disregarded, and Britain still continues business as usual, then statements about “shared democratic values” become meaningless.

Imran Khan does not need another carefully worded expression of concern.

He needs consequences for those violating his rights.

And Pakistan needs the same thing.

Make repression expensive.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.
